sources.title: Charlotte County historical-resources survey: regional cultural history
sources.note: County cultural-resources report summarizing Caloosahatchee phase dates, site types, pottery, subsistence, burial evidence, and regional boundary uncertainty.

sources.title: Marquardt and Walker, The Archaeology of Pineland
sources.note: University of Florida monograph covering excavation, chronology, house floors, artifacts, soils, human remains, environment, households, and historical interpretation at Pineland.

sources.title: Florida Museum Environmental Archaeology: Pineland
sources.note: Institutional project account of shell complexes, canal, water court, house floors, year-round settlement, plants, cordage, fauna, soils, and environmental change.

sources.title: Florida Museum: Pineland ancient landscape
sources.note: Excavation and geophysical evidence for fifth- and sixth-century occupation, postmolds, structures, midden, artifacts, and earlier shore-oriented settlement.

sources.title: Florida Museum: Pineland dark ages
sources.note: Evidence-bounded working hypothesis relating cooling, sea-level fall, fisheries change, reduced deposits, and temporary Pineland abandonment around 800 to 900.

sources.title: Florida Museum: Useppa Island geology and archaeology
sources.note: Institutional synthesis of dated occupations, burials, foods, shell-tool production, ninth-century settlement shifts, and site-specific uncertainty.

sources.title: Florida Museum: new waterlogged deposits at Pineland
sources.note: Excavation report on circa 500 to 600 pottery, wood, palm-fiber cordage, probable netting, seeds, shell tools, animal remains, nested screening, and conservation.

sources.title: Florida Museum: an ancient Pineland shoreline
sources.note: Radiocarbon-dated 1000 to 1200 shoreline deposit with cordage, knots, probable netting, seeds, wood, pottery, shell artifacts, and food remains.

sources.title: Florida Museum: where Pineland people obtained fresh water
sources.note: Archaeological and environmental evidence for artesian springs, a spring-fed creek, freshwater flow, wet deposits, and the limits of modern surface appearance.

sources.title: Florida Museum: shell mounds as middens and architecture
sources.note: Excavation-based explanation of shell, bone, charcoal, broken tools, pottery, soil, activity surfaces, and the difference between midden accumulation and deliberate fill.

sources.title: Thompson and colleagues, geoarchaeology of Mound Key
sources.note: Open peer-reviewed coring, excavation, radiocarbon, mound formation, abandonment, reoccupation, household change, cooperative labor, and environmental interpretation.

sources.title: Thompson and colleagues, ancient engineering of fish capture and storage
sources.note: Open peer-reviewed excavation, dating, hydrology, fish-scale, cordage, canal, and watercourt evidence for live-fish capture and storage at Mound Key.

sources.title: Hutchinson and colleagues, Calusa and prehistoric subsistence
sources.note: Peer-reviewed isotope, zooarchaeological, and archaeobotanical synthesis finding marine protein and C3 plants, no prehistoric maize signal, and mixed resource use.

sources.title: Lulewicz and colleagues, zooarchaeological networks at Pineland
sources.note: Open peer-reviewed study of local fish and shellfish, year-round occupation, small and multifamily households, changing environments, and the limits of causal claims.

sources.title: Thompson, Marquardt, and Walker, remote sensing at Pineland
sources.note: Peer-reviewed geophysical study of shoreline modification, canal construction, buried house patterns, changing household composition, and noninvasive survey limits.

sources.title: Marquardt and colleagues, episodic complexity and a coastal kingdom
sources.note: Peer-reviewed synthesis of Mound Key monuments, food processing, watercourts, climate, cooperation, coercion, and the late development of Calusa political complexity.

sources.title: Thompson and colleagues, collective action and the rise of the Calusa
sources.note: Peer-reviewed analysis of a repeatedly rebuilt mound-top structure, long-lived lineage, collective projects, environmental change, and later state-like formation.

sources.title: Penn Museum: Calusa maritime peoples and Key Marco excavations
sources.note: Museum account of Key Marco excavation context, house posts, nets, shell tools, vessels, canoes, pottery, masks, figureheads, ceremonial interpretation, and stratigraphic limits.

sources.title: Smithsonian SOVA: Sawyer paintings of Key Marco masks and tablets
sources.note: Authoritative archive catalog for visual documentation of masks and tablets, collection scope, 1896 context, repository, creator, and explicit no-linguistic-content designation.

sources.title: Florida Museum: Useppa shell-axe workshop fieldwork
sources.note: Excavation report on concentrated lightning-whelk debris just before 800, shell-axe production, volunteer labor, and implications for woodworking and specialization.

sources.title: Florida Museum: archaeological salvage at Browns Complex Mound 4
sources.note: Controlled salvage report on IIA through IV occupation, alternating midden and activity surfaces, burial expectations, and the documented absence of remains in the tested pit.

sources.title: Florida Museum: publication of The Archaeology of Pineland
sources.note: Institutional synthesis of the interdisciplinary Pineland project, 1,700 years of occupation, chronology, environment, artifacts, human osteology, and research scope.

sources.title: Florida State Parks: culture of Cayo Costa
sources.note: State park account of long Indigenous occupation, Caloosahatchee cultural affiliation, marine resources, middens, discarded tools, pottery, bones, and site interpretation.

sources.title: National Park Service: Everglades archaeological heritage
sources.note: Federal heritage account of southwest Florida shell works, fishing and foraging, shell and bone tools, ornaments, waterways, and historically documented Calusa settlements.

sources.title: Florida Museum: the Calusa and Randell Research Center
sources.note: Institutional account of long-term coastal life, fishing, engineered mounds, canals, watercourts, nets, canoes, regional networks, and later Calusa history.
